posts.full_text: Proximity used to be the golden rule in travel. That rule is breaking. According to EasyJet's 2026 Travel Trends Report, travellers are now trading an extra 90 minutes in the air for 2x the value on the ground. The 5-hour flight, which historically sat in no-man's land, too long for a weekend, too short for a big trip, is becoming the new sweet spot. Two things are driving this: → The flight itself has changed. High-speed WiFi and improved cabin comfort have turned those extra hours into productive or restorative time. The 5th and 6th hours are no longer dead time. → The value equation has shifted. Nearly 1 in 4 travellers now prioritise meaning over mobility. They're willing to sit a little longer to reach warmer climates, stronger currency advantages, or a more noticeable break from routine, without the jet lag or price tag of \"long-haul\". The data backs this up. Morocco, Turkey and Cyprus have seen a 21% increase in bookings from Europe. Tunisia is up 12% on its \"luxury-for-less\" positioning. Tbilisi has emerged as a top city break for 2026 thanks to new direct routes. But a destination I keep thinking about is Egypt. A few years ago, Beautiful Destinations worked with Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities - Egypt & Rania A. Al-Mashat & Ahmed Youssef on campaigns showcasing the country- the Pyramids, the Red Sea, the culture, the food, the people. At the time, Egypt was competing for attention against closer European options. Now, with this 5-hour window expanding, Egypt sits in a structurally stronger position than ever. For destination marketers, I think the strategic shift is clear: stop selling proximity. Start selling return on time. → One extra hour = a completely different climate → One extra hour = a 40% stronger currency advantage → One extra hour = a deeper cultural reset The destinations that frame themselves as \"worth the extra hour\" will win the next cycle of demand 🚀 📸 One of the best experiences of my life in Egypt after a short flight from London!

posts.full_text: I used to believe you could predict what content would work. After 12 years in this industry, I've finally accepted I was wrong. For most of my career, travel marketing operated on a simple model: shoot, pick your best content, run it everywhere. Hero content first. So we started asking a different question at Beautiful Destinations: what if we stopped trying to predict and started building AI enabled systems that learn faster? It's a polarising topic, and I understand why. Those who have followed me for a while know I'm a huge believer in the positives AI will bring to our industry. It will come as no surprise that we've been experimenting with AI that generates video from photo. Same shoot. Same REAL, authentic content. But now hundreds of visual variants, optimized for performance and tested across platforms in real-time. The shift in mindset has been humbling. I spent years trusting only my instincts on what content would resonate. Now I'm increasingly trusting a system to tell me what actually does.

posts.text:
Every major hotel brand is rethinking loyalty right now, but I’m not convinced most of them are solving the right problem 🧐

According to Squaremouth, the average cost of a vacation in 2025 was $7,249
posts.full_text:
Every major hotel brand is rethinking loyalty right now, but I’m not convinced most of them are solving the right problem 🧐

According to Squaremouth, the average cost of a vacation in 2025 was $7,249, up 24% from 2024, and the average cost of an international trip was $9,922, up 11% from 2024. Increasingly, those trips are being tied to fixed moments like concerts, finals, weddings and festivals. When the anchor is time-specific, a small disruption can wipe out the entire emotional return.

That changes what loyalty means.

For years, hospitality loyalty was built on points and upgrades. It rewarded frequency and worked in a relatively stable environment. But that environment doesn't exist in the same way anymore. Between climate volatility, airspace closures, weather systems and more, disruption has become part of the journey.

So when something goes wrong, guests aren't thinking about their bonus points.

That’s where the shift is happening. Flexible cancellation used to feel generous, but now it’s the baseline. Research from Expedia Group shows that more than 50% of travellers would abandon a booking without a refund option, and data from TravelBoom Hotel Marketing found 94% of travellers expect flexibility within their booking.

What builds loyalty now is recovery. If a flight delay risks someone missing a headline concert they've flown across the world to see, the hotel that steps in with proactive support earns something far more valuable than another stay - credibility, and credibility compounds 🙏

But that recovery can’t just extend to one person. According to Skift, 92% of travellers aren’t travelling alone, yet historically support has focused on the individual who clicked ‘book’. That disconnect matters because if one person’s trip collapses, the whole group feels it.

That gap is being closed. The Allianz and Marriott International collaboration is a great signal of what that looks like: embedding protection into the booking flow and offering coverage across the whole trip, not just the booking nights.

The bigger pattern I’m seeing is that loyalty is shifting from mechanics to emotional safety.

Points and perks still matter, but when a trip is expensive, infrequent and tied to something meaningful, what guests remember is who helped them when plans went sideways.

And the brands that design for that reality - across the entire journey, not just within four walls - are going to build a different kind of loyalty with the next generation of traveller 🥂
posts.hook: Every major hotel brand is rethinking loyalty right now, but I’m not convinced most of them are solving the right problem 🧐
posts.topic: The evolution of hotel loyalty programs from mechanics (points/upgrades) to emotional safety and proactive recovery.

posts.full_text:
There’s no doubt, it’s been a challenging week in the UAE. Made more challenging by certain media outlets, by misinformation and opportunistic reporting that, in my opinion, does not help. I’ve been a proud and vocal supporter of the UAE since I moved my family and businesses here, and I remain a proud and vocal supporter today. Even more so, as I live through their phenomenal response to recent challenges. My friend Amit Nayak, CHA wrote a great piece for Hotelier Middle East that really made me think, and I hope is helpful for anyone looking for clarity on the future of the UAE and a deeper understanding of why so many people like me are proud to call this place our home.

The UAE is the world’s third-largest humanitarian donor.

$1.46 billion contributed in a single year, behind only the United States and the European Union. Both economies are many, many times the size of the UAE's. I don't think most people in the travel industry know this. It was therefore not surprising to me when the UAE government stepped in during the first days of this year's regional disruption and offered to cover hotel and meal costs for more than 20,000 stranded passengers.

When you've lived here, spent real time here, built relationships here and worked with the government, you start to understand that gestures like this are very much part of the country's DNA. You feel safe and looked after when times are good. I feel exactly the same when times are less so.

In the travel industry we spend a lot of time talking about "guest experience". About the moments that make a destination or a hotel stay memorable. About the reality on the ground that turns a visit into something people carry with them long after they've left. I've long believed that the places that stand out most are always those where hospitality shows up in how people are treated when things are difficult. Destinations that have invested most deeply in people.

They look after their own communities and the travellers who pass through them.

That is the UAE story. It's been their story since its founding, and it will continue to be their story long into the future. I believe it deserves to be told much more widely. Amit's piece does exactly that, exploring the response to the disruption and what it says about the country's approach to hospitality.

I believe moments like this reveal something important for the wider travel industry - demand always comes back after disruption, when you act right and have laid long-term foundations.

Being here on the ground, I can tell you, the UAE clearly has.

posts.topic: The UAE's humanitarian efforts and commitment to hospitality in response to regional challenges.

posts.text: At Beautiful Destinations we’re really excited about the potential of sports tourism. Today it’s worth $700 billion globally and projected to hit $2 trillion by 2034. But most destinations are still c
posts.full_text:
At Beautiful Destinations we’re really excited about the potential of sports tourism. Today it’s worth $700 billion globally and projected to hit $2 trillion by 2034. But most destinations are still capturing a fraction of it because…

They continue to market to a traveler that doesn’t exist anymore.

They’re building strategies around match day, assuming people show up for the game, spend money near the stadium, then leave. That might have been true 10 years ago. But it hasn’t been true for a while now.

Only 69% of sports travellers say the event is why they booked the trip. The other 31% are there because of the city, the people they’re traveling with, or the experience they couldn’t get at home. And even the 62% who come for the game are staying for multiple days and spending money on things outside the event.

This means the economic return is distributed across the full trip and across the region, not concentrated in a single day or a single venue.

The audience has shifted, too. The fastest growing segment in sports tourism isn’t the fan buying a ticket to watch, but the person traveling to compete (I’ve done this myself for a Hyrox race!). Active sports tourism (people participating in races, tournaments, fitness events) is growing at 16.14% annually and already makes up 32% of the market.

But when you look at how destinations market themselves, almost everything is still designed for spectators.

This is exactly the pattern that will play out around the 2026 FIFA World Cup. 16 cities will host matches across North America, but the economic opportunity won’t be limited to those stadium locations.

The destinations that position themselves along those travel routes and give visitors reasons to stay longer or travel further will benefit equally if not more.

But that requires a very different strategy from simply promoting a stadium and an event date- something social media is tailor made for.

We think this represents such a big opportunity that we did a deep dive report that I thought you might enjoy! The BD 2026 Sports Tourism Report looks at exactly this shift and shares a playbook for how to leverage it. I’d love to hear your thoughts! 😎🙏
posts.hook: At Beautiful Destinations we’re really excited about the potential of sports tourism.
posts.topic: Sports Tourism Shifts from Spectators to Active Participants

The next wave of high-margin travel is already here, but most brands are looking in the wrong direction.

Travellers over 65 are now one of the strongest drivers of growth in travel spend. Barclay’s d
posts.full_text:
The next wave of high-margin travel is already here, but most brands are looking in the wrong direction.

Travellers over 65 are now one of the strongest drivers of growth in travel spend. Barclay’s data shows that the 65+ demographic recorded a 8.7% spend growth last year, while the 14-24 group grew just 2.9%, spending roughly a third as much.

This data is unsurprising when you look at the findings from a survey Travel Weekly reported, recording that 68% of parents with independent adult children now prefer spending on family experiences over inheritance.

The real power in travel right now sits with the ‘silver economy’: people with time and liquidity. And what I find interesting about this is how it’s playing out in content.

For this demographic, they’re not scrolling for an ‘Instagrammable’ sunset. The dream is already sold, so they want clarity on:

→ Access & Mobility: How far is the walk from the transfer to the lobby?
→ Predictability: What does the actual pace of the itinerary feel like?
→ Credibility: They favour ‘utility creators’ who act as measured, practical guides.

This shift matters for anyone working in travel right now, because this segment behaves very differently and very favourably when they book. They stay longer, they upgrade to higher room categories and they have the lowest price sensitivity in the market. That combination of high daily spend, longer duration and service priority makes them one of the highest-margin segments in tourism today 👏

The mistake many travel brands are making today is assuming social media is a young person’s channel.

If your content doesn’t answer the questions the silver economy is asking, you’re leaving one of the most profitable segments on the table.
posts.hook: The next wave of high-margin travel is already here, but most brands are looking in the wrong direction.
posts.topic: The "silver economy" (travelers 65+) as a high-margin growth driver in the travel industry.

Some destinations explode in popularity overnight, but then very quickly fade into the background. Ever wondered why? 🧐

When a destination goes viral, flights increase, hotels fill up and social feed
posts.full_text:
Some destinations explode in popularity overnight, but then very quickly fade into the background. Ever wondered why? 🧐

When a destination goes viral, flights increase, hotels fill up and social feeds get flooded with the same 'hidden gem' and 'must visit' content. But sometimes, this popularity is only short-lived.

It's a cycle I've watched repeat itself for years, and the reason it repeats is because what happens on the surface is very different from what's going on underneath. Becoming a viral sensation online is often just the 'acceleration' phase of a peak, and destinations often aren't built to sustain this.

I think this cycle is something we're going to see accelerate this year, because discovery is now digitally compressed, which means algorithms and social search can take a location from being relatively unknown to global saturation overnight. The peaks are higher, but the drop-off is much faster.

What many leaders underestimate is that while attention is fast, relevance is just as fragile.

When visibility drives volume, the 'original identity' of a destination begins to stretch. Infrastructure strains, service quality becomes inconsistent, prices rise and the original narrative gets diluted, eventually leading to the energy shifting elsewhere.

The destinations that survive this cycle are those that understand what stage of the lifecycle they're in and actively design for what comes next:

→ Instead of chasing arrivals, they're investing in evolving the narrative
→ Instead of amplifying what's already popular, they're diversifying the experience with the next generation of visual proof points.
→ And instead of fearing the drop-off, they're using data to predict and manage it.

Peak popularity is easy to celebrate. But staying relevant after the wave and building for what comes next is where the real strategy begins 🤝
posts.hook: Some destinations explode in popularity overnight, but then very quickly fade into the background. Ever wondered why? 🧐
posts.topic: The lifecycle of destination attention and strategies for staying relevant amidst social media-driven popularity cycles.

posts.full_text:
Last year, Beautiful Destinations set out to do something ambitious - to create a place where emerging talent could grow, experiment and learn the reality of modern storytelling inside one of the world’s most dynamic destinations.

Powered by the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, we did exactly that, creating the Beautiful Destinations Academy. And today, Cohorts 2 and 3 have officially graduated.

Seeing that room full of talent ready to step into the industry was a big moment for all of us.

When we built the Academy, the thinking was simple. Content matters now more than ever within the travel industry, yet very few destinations are investing properly in the people who create it.

After over a decade in this industry, we know that great creators aren’t born from nothing. They need real pressure, briefs and feedback. So we brought them to Dubai and gave them exactly that 🫡

For 12 weeks, these cohorts worked on live projects tied to major moments like Dubai Fitness Challenge, UNTOLD and PFL. They were out in the desert at sunrise, in Michelin-starred kitchens at night, on fast-moving shoots that demanded speed and precision, and they had to operate at the standard our partners expect.

By the end of it, you could really see the transformation. These cohorts refined their skills, turning early edits into sharper storytelling and replacing hesitation with confidence. And by the end of it, the final films felt ready to take on the global stage.

A big thank you to Issam Kazim, Weera (Shahwir) Saad Hassan and the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, who have continued to support this academy as part of a bigger ambition under D33 to position Dubai as a hub for creative talent. That kind of long-term thinking is rare, and it’s why this programme works.

A massive congratulations again to Cohorts 2 and 3 on the work you’ve done and for continuing to raise the bar 💅🏼

As the global interest in the academy keeps increasing, it shows you just how important this kind of talent has become for destinations across the globe.

And with the level of talent it’s producing only one year in, I know we’ve only scratched the surface of what’s to come!
posts.hook: Last year, Beautiful Destinations set out to do something ambitious - to create a place where emerging talent could grow, experiment and learn the reality of modern storytelling inside one of the world’s most dynamic destinations.
posts.topic: The graduation of Cohorts 2 and 3 from the Beautiful Destinations Academy in Dubai.

posts.text: Most travel content gets liked, but very little of it actually gets someone to book. So how do you close that gap?\n\nTravel content has moved from aspiration to action, and for the first time, that j
posts.full_text:
Most travel content gets liked, but very little of it actually gets someone to book. So how do you close that gap?

Travel content has moved from aspiration to action, and for the first time, that journey is measurable.

Currently, aspirational, 'dreaming' style content, which is emotional and shows a destination's essence in a digestible way, is driving the most passive engagement on social media. But it's not where decisions are made.

Decisions are made inside 'planning' content that helps users decide where to visit, what to do and how to do it. This kind of content focuses on tangible value and advice, such as itineraries or local guides, and it's generating far more saves than any other kind of travel content on social media right now, which has become the strongest signal of intent across multiple platforms 👏

Travellers are increasingly bookmarking posts and sharing them privately in DMs, turning moments of scrolling into moments of decision-making. I think what's especially interesting is how platforms are optimising for this kind of behaviour now by prioritising intent signals like saves and DMs as a signal of content value.

That's why I believe that the most valuable travel content this year will be content that users perceive to be the most useful, because social media has matured from a discovery channel to a decision-support system. Not just for travellers, but for brands, destinations and operators trying to influence real outcomes.

This year, if your content only exists to inspire, you'll win attention and awareness, but you might lose the booking. The brands that are winning are the ones building content for people to return to, save and share when they're actively planning, not just scrolling.

This is just one of the trends we've seen this year from our Beautiful Destinations Social Media Trends Report for 2026. This report is everything you need as a brand, destination or CMO to survive on social media this year. Read the report here: https://lnkd.in/ey_NHUNK
posts.hook: Most travel content gets liked, but very little of it actually gets someone to book. So how do you close that gap?
posts.topic: Social media travel content strategy: The shift from 'dreaming' to 'planning' content to drive bookings.

America isn’t just preparing for a World Cup year in 2026. It’s preparing to bridge the gap between its iconic host cities and regional tourism growth.

Brand USA’s ‘America the Beautiful’ campaign is
posts.full_text:
America isn’t just preparing for a World Cup year in 2026. It’s preparing to bridge the gap between its iconic host cities and regional tourism growth.

Brand USA’s ‘America the Beautiful’ campaign is one of the most strategically timed destination campaigns I’ve seen for a while. The campaign was released just as the U.S. is about to experience an unprecedented period of global attention. With the FIFA World Cup expected to generate 1.2M+ international visitors, America’s 250th anniversary and the Route 66 Centennial all happening within 2026, the challenge isn’t just awareness, but intent.

And that’s where this campaign is smart.

Rather than selling the U.S. as a checklist of landmarks, America the Beautiful reframes the country as a shared emotional experience. It shifts the proposition from ‘visit America’ to ‘feel America’, through people, culture, landscapes and everyday moments that make the country what it is.

Major global events don’t automatically translate into repeat visits or long-term tourism value. They create spikes in attention, and what defines success is what you’re able to do with that.

- High-production film gives it cinematic weight, cutting through the noise of standard tourism ads
- Connected TV and digital distribution ensure scale
- And the rollout across nine priority international markets, including India, Japan, the UK, Mexico and South Korea, shows a disciplined understanding of inbound growth potential

And early testing shows it’s working, with 72% of respondents reacting positively and 67% reporting an increased desire to visit, according to Brand USA.

It’s a brilliant example of an anticipatory campaign that arrives before the surge, shapes perception early and builds an emotional connection that lasts beyond the impact of a big sporting event. Having lived in the US for a good part of my career, I know firsthand how many amazing tourism experiences exist there.

Congrats to Fred Dixon, Leah Chandler, CDME and the Brand USA team on this one. I’m excited to see how this campaign performs as the world’s attention turns to the US in 2026 👏
posts.hook: America isn’t just preparing for a World Cup year in 2026.
posts.topic: Brand USA's 'America the Beautiful' tourism campaign for the 2026 World Cup and beyond.

With Black Summer bushfires i
posts.full_text:
A lot of people question whether tourism marketing is a cost or an investment, but I think the team at Tourism Australia have answered that question pretty convincingly.

With Black Summer bushfires in 2019, followed by an almost immediate global shutdown, Australian tourism has seen some of the toughest conditions our industry has faced. But instead of pulling back during difficult conditions, backed by Tourism Australia’s CMO Susan Coghill, they doubled down.

Five years on and I think the results speak for themselves 👏

Australia has welcomed over 8 million visitors, delivered a $14 return for every $1 spent on marketing and is now tracking towards 10 million arrivals, with 11.8 projected by 2029.

Susan has been instrumental in driving this growth through various initiatives, including their ‘Come and say G’day’ campaign. What I think this campaign gets right is its consistency at the brand level. Instead of being reinvented every year, the core idea has been compounded, allowing the brand to stay intact while the storytelling flexes locally.

The Robert Irwin activation in the U.S. is a great example. Perfectly timed around his Dancing with the Stars feature, so it’s culturally relevant, but still unmistakably part of the same global idea, helping to push the campaign past 100 million global views and contributing to a 22% spike in booking intent.

A quick look at Tourism Australia’s ‘Australia’ account on Instagram and you’ll see they are nailing social too :)

Consistency is an undervalued asset in marketing, and Susan has been instrumental in ensuring this campaign kept the core idea intact while letting each market see itself reflected in the storytelling.

Tourism marketing is an investment with a measurable multiplier, and Susan and the team at Tourism Australia give us a great example of how destination marketing drives economic value, with the compounding effect of that approach now being very visible 🤝 🚀

posts.full_text:
For a long time luxury travel has been defined by speed. How far you could go, how fast you could get there and how many places you could tick off. But I think that definition is broken. 

Rail and slow travel are rising because time itself has become a luxury. 

Explore’s 2026 travel trends show rail journey bookings jumped 77% within just 12 weeks, and forward bookings are up 41% year-on-year 👏

The appeal is about the autonomy of the experience. People want more control of their own experience, and rail is a deliberate choice that facilitates that, and I think we’re going to see a lot more of it this year. 

Because rail offers something flights increasingly can’t:
→ Your journey is part of the trip, not dead time between destinations
→ City-centre to city-centre travel and fewer friction points
→ Long, uninterrupted periods of time to think, rest or work, which is something I think will become even more important as remote and flexible work increases

What used to be framed as ‘slower’ is now being repositioned as ‘more intentional’. 

But there’s a secondary effect here that I think more destinations should be paying close attention to. 

Slow travel naturally redistributes demand. It pulls visitors beyond the obvious capitals or hot spots, encourages longer stays and unlocks secondary cities and regions without the environmental or financial cost of building new infrastructure. For destinations struggling with overtourism, this is one of the most effective levers available. 

Japan is a great example. Regions like Kyushu leaned into rail-led journeys and ritualised experiences like onsen culture, targeting what they identified as the ‘deep experience’ traveller. The result? They increased the average stay length by 22% in regions that built narrative-driven rail itineraries, compared to 8% growth in fly-in/fly-out gateway cities. 

For destinations living in the shadow of a major capital, this is an opportunity to capture a segment that spends more, stays longer and distributes more evenly across regions. Rail-led slow travel might be the most powerful repositioning tool and demand-shaping strategy you have.
posts.hook: For a long time luxury travel has been defined by speed.
posts.topic: The rise of slow and intentional rail travel as a new definition of luxury and a tool against overtourism.

posts.full_text:
I am fascinated by how quickly travel marketing is changing with AI.

I know I’m writing about it a lot on LinkedIn, but it’s largely because today reminds me so much of a decade ago, when social media was changing how consumers discovered travel, and travel marketers were slow to react.

Last week, OpenAI confirmed it was testing ads inside ChatGPT and I think the impact for us in travel will be profound.

LLMs don’t sit at the end of the journey like search or OTAs. They’re right up at the start, with social. They sit at what I think is the most influential moment of all: when someone is forming their mental shortlist and looking for what is possible.

For many of us, they are far, far better than what we’ve been used to. At the discovery stage of travel when I don’t know exactly where I want to go yet, LLMs don’t give me links, they give me guidance. My whole “search” experience has changed, as questions drive my process:

→ Where should I go in April if I want warm weather but fewer crowds?
→ Is Tokyo or Seoul better for a first-time solo trip for my adult mother?
→ What’s a good alternative to Paris that is only 2 hours away from London?

When an answer appears in that moment, framed with context and confidence, it defines the options people consider and has a far greater influence on how intent is formed in the first place.

As Skift highlighted, travel is already one of the most common categories people ask ChatGPT about, whether it’s destinations, itineraries, timings or comparisons. That means fewer touchpoints overall but far more influence per question.

For travel brands and destinations, I think this raises some big questions:

→ What kinds of questions do you want to be the answer to?
→ How clearly does your brand stand for a specific outcome, traveller type or use case?
→ How easy is your story to understand to an AI that’s optimising for relevance, trust and clarity?

And the most important question of all - when an LLM has recommended you at this early stage of the decision-making process, do you have all the requisite rich video assets to bring that text-based search to life and convert the user’s interest?

This shift is less about buying attention and more about earning inclusion in the moment when decisions are converted in the formats users want to see. And for an industry built on emotion, reassurance and long-term consideration, I think that’s a shift we all need to be paying close attention to.

Curious to hear whether you’re already optimising for conversational discovery or just mainly for search? 🤔
posts.hook: I am fascinated by how quickly travel marketing is changing with AI.
posts.topic: The impact of AI and LLMs on travel marketing and conversational discovery.

posts.full_text:
For years, I’ve watched travel brands treat creators as a marketing expense. But Klook just sent the clearest signal that the era of the creator-as-vendor is over.

Klook have announced that they’re hiring a ‘Chief Spring Officer’ - a role responsible for how spring travel is seen and experienced in real time, from surfacing the best experiences to reacting to weather shifts, crowd density and bloom progression.

Spring is a huge season for tourism in Japan, driven by the iconic cherry blossom (sakura) season, which drove a record 3.91 million arrivals in April 2025, up almost 30% year-on-year, and an estimated ¥1.39 trillion in economic impact, the highest in Japan’s history. When demand moves like that, how people understand the moment is as important as the moment itself.

Klook is getting ahead of that by bringing creator strategy into the C-Suite to sit alongside its continued focus on experience-led discovery and travel intelligence. It also plugs directly into their wider ‘Kreator’ program, which has scaled to 20,000+ members and sees roughly 30% conversion from content, surpassing the 20% benchmark of global competitors.

The key takeaway for brands and tourism boards is this: you can’t bolt creators onto a traditional structure and expect outsized returns. If creators are genuinely outperforming ads, then product, partnerships, data and seasonal planning all need to move closer to them.

Big congrats to Ethan Lin, Eric Gnock Fah, Bernie Xiaokang Xiong and the entire team at Klook on this success. This is a smart move, and I’m excited to see where you take it next 😎
posts.hook: For years, I’ve watched travel brands treat creators as a marketing expense.
posts.topic: Klook hiring a 'Chief Spring Officer' and the shift towards creator-led travel strategy.

Last week, Kerry Healy wrote an article about something I think a lot of hospitality brands still underestimate."
""
"The shift from simply showing a place to helping someone feel it. And that shift matters a lot more than most brands realise."
""
"Kerry talked about how a single piece of visual content changed how she saw Dubai. Instead of a checklist of landmarks, it became a place with layers and moments that you don’t always get from a brochure, and that really resonated with me because it’s the exact shift we’ve been building towards for years."
""
"And it’s exactly the thinking that sits behind the strategic partnership between Beautiful Destinations and Accor - to reshape consumer perceptions and enhance brand visibility through dynamic and personalised content creation. Our ‘From Dusk To Dawn’ project spans 21 destinations and 67 hotels across Asia, the Pacific and the Middle East, with more on the way, to showcase culturally rich experiences within and beyond hotel walls. "
""
"That’s the power of great storytelling - it creates curiosity and gives your brain just enough material to start imagining yourself there. You begin to picture how you’d visit a destination and what kind of experience you’d actually have there, and that’s what makes a destination feel personal 👏 "
""
"What I loved most in Kerry’s reflection is her point about familiarity. Seeing Australia, her home country, through a different creative lens made familiar places feel new again. That’s the possibility with story-led content - one piece of content can change how you think about a place you thought you already understood."
""
"And this is where a lot of brands underestimate the value of content, because it’s not something you just layer on top of a campaign."
""
"In reality, content is often the very beginning of someone’s discovery journey. It’s the moment where curiosity and intent form, long before anyone is looking at prices or availability."
""
"And that’s the real challenge for hospitality now. How do you create that feeling across brands, markets and cultures, without losing the human edge?"
""
"Hospitality has always been emotional, and visual storytelling is how that emotion travels."
""
"A huge thank you to Kerry, Victoria Sertic and the team for their support and amazing partnership. We cannot wait for what is next!

France has officially secured its spot as the most visited destination in 2025, but it’s currently ranking 4th for tourism spend. "
""
"Despite welcoming 28.6M less people, the U.S. generated roughly $138B more in tourism spend than France according to the latest data available. "
""
"That gap is huge, and I think it tells us a few very important things about tourism: "
""
"→  High-spend travellers beat high volume. "
"The top-earning destinations prioritise long-haul visitors, longer stays and higher daily spend. Countries like the U.S., Australia and the UK benefit from travellers who spend across retail, food, entertainment and experiences."
""
"→  Tourism works best when it serves multiple purposes. "
"The strongest economies don’t rely on leisure alone. They combine tourism with business travel, education, conferences, major events and visiting friends and family. These multi-purpose trips increase total spend and dramatically improve repeat visitation."
""
"→  Big earners sell experiences. "
"Destinations that invest in live entertainment, cultural institutions, sporting events and attractions can justify higher prices and longer stays. People pay more because the experience feels worth it."
""
"→  Strong domestic infrastructure multiplies value. "
"High-earning countries have efficient internal air, rail and urban transport networks that allow travellers to move easily beyond a single hotspot. That spreads spending across regions and unlocks secondary cities that might otherwise be overlooked."
""
"→  Pricing power is the real differentiator. "
"The countries earning the most from tourism don’t rely on heavy discounting. They protect value through brand perception, quality, consistency and trust. That’s what allows them to sustain margins even in volatile markets."
""
"The biggest lesson for destination leaders is this: growth without value is fragile."
""
"The countries earning the most from tourism built systems that make every visit worth more - economically, culturally and emotionally. That’s how tourism scales sustainably 😎
posts.hook: France has officially secured its spot as the most visited destination in 2025, but it’s currently ranking 4th for tourism spend. "

"It also sends a powerful trust signal, because only the brands that truly understand their value can afford to lean into negative perceptions like this and be this playful with their reputation."
""

posts.full_text:
Right now, everyone’s racing to rebuild their travel strategies around AI, but 75% of travellers still don’t trust AI. "
""
"I use AI all day everyday and it is brilliant at helping people think about travel, but it’s still struggling to help them commit. "
""
"What we’re seeing is a disconnect between discovery and transaction. "
""
"Travellers are happy to use AI to explore destinations and narrow down options, but when it actually comes to booking flights or hotels, trust drops quickly. According to Insider Travel Report, less than 20% of U.S. markets trust AI for transactions, and IDC has predicted that by 2030, only 30% of travel bookings will be completed by AI agents."
""
"I don’t think this is a technology problem, but more of a human nature and accountability one. "
""
"When something goes wrong in travel, like delays or cancellations, people want to know who’s responsible. So while AI can suggest and optimise, it can’t yet provide people with the reassurance they’re looking for when money and experiences are on the line. "
""
"Currently, travellers are using AI to do a lot of the heavy lifting, then switching to human-verified platforms to validate the decision before they pay, and this creates a disconnect for a lot of brands. So on one side, teams are optimising for AI, but on the other, consumer behaviour hasn’t fully caught up to the point of conversion. "
""
"But the bit I think is especially important is how that gap isn’t uniform globally. Markets like China, Saudi Arabia and India are adopting AI far faster than the U.S. or parts of Europe, which means a single global AI strategy won’t work. "
""
"Right now, I don’t think the smart move is to pick one side or the other. I think it’s to run a dual-track strategy:"
""
"→ Optimise for AI discovery, because early movers will own high-intent questions when behaviour shifts"
"→ But keep the trusted, human-led conversion points while confidence is still fragile"
""
"Trust is the most expensive commodity in travel, and it’s not something you can automate overnight. "
""
"I’m curious to hear from leaders in this space. How is this gap between discovery and transaction impacting how you’re handling travellers? And how long do you think it will be before AI fully automates everything? 🙏
posts.hook: Right now, everyone’s racing to rebuild their travel strategies around AI, but 75% of travellers still don’t trust AI. "

"Traditionally, hotels compete on rooms, destinations on attractions, and airlines on routes."

""
"And that’s where premium value is being created now 👏"
""
"To me, this signals a broader shift I’m seeing across the industry:"
""
"→ From selling places to designing environments "
""
"→ From transactional stays to relational experiences "
""
"→ From itinerary building to orchestrating an entire ecosystem"
""

posts.full_text:
America isn’t just preparing for a World Cup year in 2026. It’s preparing to bridge the gap between its iconic host cities and regional tourism growth. "
""
"Brand USA’s ‘America the Beautiful’ campaign is one of the most strategically timed destination campaigns I’ve seen for a while. The campaign was released just as the U.S. is about to experience an unprecedented period of global attention. With the FIFA World Cup expected to generate 1.2M+ international visitors, America’s 250th anniversary and the Route 66 Centennial all happening within 2026, the challenge isn’t just awareness, but intent. "
""
"And that’s where this campaign is smart. "
""
"Rather than selling the U.S. as a checklist of landmarks, America the Beautiful reframes the country as a shared emotional experience. It shifts the proposition from ‘visit America’ to ‘feel America’, through people, culture, landscapes and everyday moments that make the country what it is. "
""
"Major global events don’t automatically translate into repeat visits or long-term tourism value. They create spikes in attention, and what defines success is what you’re able to do with that attention."
""
"This campaign is designed to bridge that gap:"
""
"- High-production film gives it cinematic weight, cutting through the noise of standard tourism ads"
"- Connected TV and digital distribution ensure scale"
"- And the rollout across nine priority international markets, including India, Japan, the UK, Mexico and South Korea, shows a disciplined understanding of inbound growth potential "
""
"And early testing shows it's working, with 72% of respondents reacting positively and 67% reporting an increased desire to visit, according to Brand USA. "
""

posts.full_text:
I am fascinated by how quickly travel marketing is changing with AI. "
""
"I know I’m writing about it a lot on LinkedIn, but it’s largely because today reminds me so much of a decade ago, when social media was changing how consumers discovered travel, and travel marketers were slow to react."
""
"Last week, OpenAI confirmed it was testing ads inside ChatGPT and I think the impact for us in travel will be profound."
""
"LLMs don’t sit at the end of the journey like search or OTAs. They’re right up at the start, with social. They sit at what I think is the most influential moment of all: when someone is forming their mental shortlist and looking for what is possible. "
""
"For many of us, they are far, far better than what we’ve been used to. At the discovery stage of travel when I don’t know exactly where I want to go yet, LLMs don't give me links, they give me guidance. My whole “search” experience has changed, as questions drive my process:"
""
"→ Where should I go in April if I want warm weather but fewer crowds?"
"→ Is Tokyo or Seoul better for a first-time solo trip for my adult mother?"
"→ What’s a good alternative to Paris that is only 2 hours away from London? "
""
"When an answer appears in that moment, framed with context and confidence, it defines the options people consider and has a far greater influence on how intent is formed in the first place. "
""
"As Skift highlighted, travel is already one of the most common categories people ask ChatGPT about, whether it's destinations, itineraries, timings or comparisons. That means fewer touchpoints overall but far more influence per question. "
""
"For travel brands and destinations, I think this raises some big questions:"
""
"→ What kinds of questions do you want to be the answer to?"
"→ How clearly does your brand stand for a specific outcome, traveller type or use case? "
"→ How easy is your story to understand to an AI that's optimising for relevance, trust and clarity?"
""
"And the most important question of all - when an LLM has recommended you at this early stage of the decision-making process, do you have all the requisite rich video assets to bring that text-based search to life and convert the user's interest?"
""
"This shift is less about buying attention and more about earning inclusion in the moment when decisions are converted in the formats users want to see. And for an industry built on emotion, reassurance and long-term consideration, I think that’s a shift we all need to be paying close attention to. "
""
"Curious to hear whether you’re already optimising for conversational discovery or just mainly for search? 🤔
posts.hook: I am fascinated by how quickly travel marketing is changing with AI. "

posts.full_text:
Most travel content gets liked, but very little of it actually gets someone to book. So how do you close that gap?"
""
"Travel content has moved from aspiration to action, and for the first time, that journey is measurable."
""
"Currently, aspirational, ‘dreaming’ style content, which is emotional and shows a destination’s essence in a digestible way, is driving the most passive engagement on social media. But it’s not where decisions are made."
""
"Decisions are made inside ‘planning’ content that helps users decide where to visit, what to do and how to do it. This kind of content focuses on tangible value and advice, such as itineraries or local guides, and it’s generating far more saves than any other kind of travel content on social media right now, which has become the strongest signal of intent across multiple platforms 👏"
""
"Travellers are increasingly bookmarking posts and sharing them privately in DMs, turning moments of scrolling into moments of decision-making. I think what’s especially interesting is how platforms are optimising for this kind of behaviour now by prioritising intent signals like saves and DMs as a signal of content value."
""
"That’s why I believe that the most valuable travel content this year will be content that users perceive to be the most useful, because social media has matured from a discovery channel to a decision-support system. Not just for travellers, but for brands, destinations and operators trying to influence real outcomes."
""
"This year, if your content only exists to inspire, you’ll win attention and awareness, but you might lose the booking. The brands that are winning are the ones building content for people to return to, save and share when they’re actively planning, not just scrolling."
""
"This is just one of the trends we’ve seen this year from our Beautiful Destinations Social Media Trends Report for 2026. This report is everything you need as a brand, destination or CMO to survive on social media this year. Read the report here: https://lnkd.in/ey_NHUNK
posts.hook: Most travel content gets liked, but very little of it actually gets someone to book. So how do you close that gap?"

posts.full_text:
Google’s live translation update might look like a small AI feature to most. For travel, it’s anything but. It’s a great example of another development in what AI can do, but I think its real significance for travel lies in its cultural impact. "
""
"I grew up with a Spanish-speaking Colombian mother and an English-speaking Scottish father - a multi-lingual household that I always saw as a huge advantage. For most, language is one of the biggest invisible barriers we experience in travel, because when travellers can’t communicate, we don’t engage. We observe, we photograph, we consume, but then move on."
""
"Live translation removes that friction almost entirely. And when you remove that friction, I think you stop passing through places and start participating in them. "
""
"Just imagine the fundamental shift in your trip if you could speak to a local shop owner, restauranteur or stranger in the hotel lobby. Suddenly, smaller towns and lesser-known regions where translation isn’t traditionally available suddenly become entirely accessible to you. "
""
"This is going to have real implications for our industry. Here’s how I think it will unfold:"
""
"- For travellers, it will open the door to micro-travel experiences and deeper cultural connections, shifting the traveller’s role from a passive observer to an active participant. I think this is fantastic and goes to the root of why I love to travel so much."
""
"- For destination marketers - it becomes a massive opportunity for destinations that don’t traditionally benefit from mass tourism, while also reducing the pressure on hyper-touristed areas by redistributing demand toward places that were previously overlooked because they didn’t feel ‘easy’ to navigate. Am I being idealistic? Maybe. But if a person feels more confident to explore because a major barrier to communication is removed I think that’s a good thing."
""
"This development aligns closely with the trends I’ve been seeing over the past year from travellers who are choosing destinations based on emotional connection and experiences deeply rooted in culture. This technology facilitates that, but on a much larger scale. "
""
"It’ll never be about replacing human interaction, more blending technology to better enable it. When language stops being a barrier, the map of global tourism starts to expand. And to me that’s a great thing :)

posts.full_text:
The biggest unlock I’ve discovered in my entrepreneurial journey is tracking and understanding my health data."
""
"At the Global Wellness Summit, my conversation with Dr Kristen Holmes PhD, Global Head of Human Performance at WHOOP, revealed something that’s becoming increasingly important for anyone who travels, works across time zones or operates at a high level: small data-driven improvements in your health have outsized improvements in your life."
""
"We’ve had access to health data for so many years, but what’s new is that technology finally knows what to do with it."
""
"Two people can live the same life on paper and still need completely different interventions. And even for the same person, the right decision yesterday might not be the right decision today."
""
"That’s the power of personalised data, it adapts as fast as you do."
""
"For someone like me who spends a lot of time travelling between countries, that level of precision is becoming essential. Because when your environment changes constantly, you need systems that can understand what your body is doing in real time."
""
"And having those systems means you spend less time guessing what your routine should look like and more time doing what’s important with energy and longevity."
""
"That’s the real opportunity, for technology not just to track your life, but to improve it too."
""
"As tools like WHOOP become more sophisticated, I think we’re going to see a huge shift in how high performers, especially those who travel, manage their days, sleep, stress and long-term health. I know my behaviours have changed dramatically recently- and I cofounded a digital health company focused on wearables data, so I thought I was in the know!"
""
"For the travel industry, there’s a big question to explore: what happens when travellers start expecting this level of precision everywhere, from airlines and hotels to wellness destinations? I think it’s only a matter of time."
""
"I’d love to hear your thoughts. If you use a tool like WHOOP, how has the personalisation changed the way you manage your life?
posts.hook: The biggest unlock I’ve discovered in my entrepreneurial journey is tracking and understanding my health data."

posts.full_text:
I love Skift's Megatrends. Every year they deliver. Every year they set the tone for the possibilities coming in our industry, and every year I like to share my favourite takes."
""
"But this year, these shifts feel less like trends and more like permanent shifts."
""
"What’s changing isn’t just where people go, but the entire journey of how discovery happens, how loyalty is earned and where travel brands fit into our daily lives. As I shared last week, I think these are generational changes that will shift the travel landscape more in the coming weeks and months than in prior decades."
""
"Digging into the report, these three trends in particular stood out to me - they speak to the shifts I’ve been seeing and talking about in travel last year,  fundamentally changing the rules of decision-making across the industry."
""
"AI and large language models will dominate our discourse in 2026. With 18% of 25-34-year-olds already using AI for holiday inspiration, are we seeing a real shift in the gatekeeper of travel? Visibility now must be about being readable to machines, and if AI doesn’t understand your core concept or what you’re known for, you simply won’t exist in that moment of decision. Don’t make the mistake so many did in the early days of social and ignore it. You’ll pay a hefty price down the road."
""
"“Loyalty” is becoming more fleeting than ever. We’re seeing a rise in ‘loyalty mercenaries’ - travellers who move fluidly across brands based on context and relevance, which means traditional loyalty is weakening and relevance is taking its place. Loyalty has shifted from something you earn over time and with frequency to something you earn in the moment by being the right fit with the right kind of content for your consumer."
""
"Connected stays extend further into your customers’ lives than ever before. Hospitality is dissolving its boundaries, with brands no longer competing solely at the point of check-in, but between trips and in everyday life. If your brand only shows up during the check-in and check-out window, you’re invisible for 95% of the customer journey. More than ever, your digital brand (social + AI) is your most constant, most extendable asset."
""
"I think these shifts are signals that the travel industry is moving from distribution-led thinking to system-led thinking."
""
"I’ve found the most value in SKIFT’s megatrends reports by compounding them over the years and trying to extrapolate out where we’re headed next. Thanks as always to Rafat Ali and Jason Clampet for setting the tone and to Sarah Kopit, Seth Borko and the team for keeping us educated and updated.

2026 will be the era of ‘whycations’ in travel. "
""
"The psychology of the consumer has fundamentally changed. For a long time, it was about escape, getting away from work or routine. "
""
"But in 2026, I think travel will become something else entirely. It’ll be about curation, identity, emotional regulation and memories - something far more active. "
""
"According to the latest data from Booking.com and Hilton, we’ve entered an era of ‘Whycation’. People aren’t just choosing a place and booking it, they’re starting with a specific emotional purpose.  "
""
"And I’ve seen that shift is showing up clearly in the data and in how people are planning, saving and booking trips, with research suggesting that 56-78% of global travellers claim that their primary motivation for booking is a specific emotional need, meaning the location has become secondary to what it can provide."
""
"From wellness-led escapes to after-dark experiences and nostalgia-driven travel, we’re seeing the motivation behind travel become deeply personal and a tool for building a better version of our reality instead of hiding from it. "
""
"This matters for destinations and brands because when travel becomes an expression of identity, the old playbook stops working and checklists and generic itineraries aren’t enough anymore. Destinations and brands have to understand the ‘why’ behind the booking.
posts.hook: 2026 will be the era of ‘whycations’ in travel. "

posts.full_text:
When people talk about the impact of travel, they usually focus on what’s visible, such as flights, hotels, arrivals, or visitor numbers. "
""
"But some of the most important contributions of the travel industry happen where most people aren’t looking. "
""
"Global travel contributes roughly to 10% of global GDP and supports around 1 in 10 jobs. That’s a huge number comparable to other industries, with travel producing 7x more jobs than the automotive industry and 4x more than the global banking sector. The World Travel & Tourism Council reported that for every direct job globally, a total of three jobs are created on an indirect or induced basis. That scale matters, but what matters more is where that money flows and who it reaches. "
""
"Behind every trip is a network of industries, communities and systems that benefit in ways most people never see and have nothing to do with ‘tourism’ as most people know it. "
""
"From supporting small-scale farmers and preserving traditional crafts to funding heritage conservation and accelerating infrastructure that locals rely on every day, travel acts as a multiplier far beyond tourism itself. "
""
"Travel is not a perfect industry, and it carries real responsibility. But when done right and with intention, travel can be one of the most powerful forces for economic resilience, cultural preservation and shared opportunity.
posts.hook: When people talk about the impact of travel, they usually focus on what’s visible, such as flights, hotels, arrivals, or visitor numbers. "

posts.full_text:
A few years ago, before AI exploded, I had a thesis about social commerce in travel, but I was wrong."
""
"I was convinced that social media would become the singular point of sale for travel. People would see the destination, share it with their decision-making circle, and as the platforms are so easy to use, that would be it. Booking done. By analysing Chinese traveller and social media behaviour (Little Red Book and Mafengwo specifically) I thought it was only a matter of time before the rest of the travel world adopted social commerce like they had."
""
"But that hasn’t really happened at scale, and I think a lot about why. It’s obvious that because travel is one of the most considered purchases a consumer will make, taking up to 69 days to go from inspiration to booking, and the complexities that exist around booking haven’t been overcome by the ease of use of social, but maybe there’s another bigger factor that I hadn’t considered."
""
"This year social media and AI together have become a far more effective sales engine, collapsing the funnel and flipping the old search-dominated model on its head."
""
"At Beautiful Destinations, we’ve been watching this play out with interest. Travel CMOs that are seeing the best results are the ones that are building full-journey content systems that answer practical questions at each stage, giving consumers the confidence they need to move from discovery to booking in these new channels."
""
"These leaders are:"
""
"- Creating video content based on trending searches in AI"
"- ⁠Making video itineraries from social listening & social trend data  "
"- Partnering deeper with OTAs & B2B travel tech providers on products that build on social search, like Expedia Group’s Trip Matching or TikTok Go with Booking.com. "
""
"So the question for every travel marketer today is: are you building content for this new customer journey or are you doing what you’ve always done?"
""
"If you’re building social content without thinking about its role in the rest of the decision-making journey, you’re handing the advantage to those that understand how AI and social media together are changing traveller behaviour. "
""
"The opportunity is shifting to a completely different way of selling travel. I’d love to hear from travel marketers who are exploring this space. Are you seeing what we are? Any insights or ideas you can share?
posts.hook: A few years ago, before AI exploded, I had a thesis about social commerce in travel, but I was wrong."

posts.full_text:
For years, the travel industry has measured success by looking backwards."
""
"Arrivals, occupancy, spend, satisfaction - all of these tell us what's already happened. But in 2026, tracking who’s arrived won’t be the most valuable metric to understand. I think tracking who’s getting ready to arrive will be."
""
"The future of travel marketing is predictive, and it’s a major shift we’re seeing across the industry right now with travellers adopting what Skyscanner calls a ‘made-for-me’ mindset, and building personalised itineraries from search, social and creators long before they even book a trip."
""
"Here are the intent signals I think travel marketers need to be measuring in 2026:"
""
"→ Save rates on social content"
"A save is one of the strongest indicators of future travel behaviour, because people save destinations or hotels when they’re considering them or starting to plan/research, not just because they like them."
""
"→ TikTok travel trends"
"Social media has the power to make a destination viral overnight, so when an itinerary or destination starts trending on platforms like TikTok (often the earliest place to discover new travel trends), it has the power to reshape demand within days, long before it shows up in arrival data."
""
"→ AI travel queries"
"The number of travellers using AI as part of their search journey is increasing rapidly, and their prompts reveal emerging patterns in the experiences they value and the cities they’re comparing. It’s demand forecasting in real time, and lots of great companies are springing up to help travel marketers tap into this."
""
"→ Wishlists and ‘dream trip’ behaviours on Pinterest"
"Pinterest feels like a sleeping giant in travel to me. Very rarely talked about but delivering impressive numbers, with over 1 billion travel-related searches and over 10 billion saves on travel-related pins recorded within one year. "
""
"People are publicly curating their next holiday months in advance, sharing the emotional drivers behind the destination choice long before price or logistics are even considered."
""
"Simply put, if you measure this early, you can allocate budget more efficiently, launch campaigns at the exact moment interest peaks, prepare experiences in advance and shape how travellers discover and book."
""
"That’s the power of intent from social. It tells you what’s about to happen, and in 2026 that will become one of the biggest competitive advantages you can have 🙏"
""
"I’m curious to know what intent signals you’re already tracking, if any? And which ones are you seeing have the biggest impact?
posts.hook: For years, the travel industry has measured success by looking backwards."

posts.full_text:
Being 15 minutes late for a flight that costs you $70 could actually end up costing an airline upwards of $1,500… "
""
"Aviation is one of the most tightly coordinated industries in the world. So when one person shows up late to the gate, it triggers a chain reaction across several other departments. "
""
"Here’s what actually happens behind the scenes when you’re late for a flight 👇"
""
"1.⁠ ⁠Gate Operations - the first ripple"
"When you’re late, the gate team has to make time-sensitive decisions that affect dispatch, load control, crew operations, baggage handlers and air traffic control. Every one of these teams is running on strict timelines, and a single delay can force everyone to recalculate. "
""
"Airlines for America estimated that in 2024, the average cost of an aircraft's operations was roughly $100.76 per minute, meaning a 15-minute passenger delay can cost up to $1,511.40. "
""
"2.⁠ ⁠Aircraft turnaround - one of the tightest workflows in aviation"
"Delays can disrupt refuelling schedules, baggage reconciliation, weight and balance calculations, cabin prep and safety checks. These processes can’t just speed back up because each airline has its own set of safety protocols and checklists that have to be completed in sequence and signed off. "
""
"3.⁠ ⁠Departure slots - miss one, miss the window"
"At airports like Heathrow or JFK, slot allocation is managed according to a tight schedule. While there’s some flexibility for minor delays, extended boarding delays can create scheduling conflicts later down the line and set off a domino effect across an airport, such as losing priority on the runway and burning additional fuel and time. "
""
"4.⁠ ⁠Crew duty-time limits"
"Federal regulations strictly limit crew flight and duty times. A series of delays throughout the day can push crews towards regulatory limits, potentially resulting in a replacement crew (if one is available at that airport). "
""
"5.⁠ ⁠The commercial cost: where it gets expensive"
"Every minute costs airlines money. Labour costs alone account for $35.23 per minute and fuel $33.06 per minute, plus maintenance and aircraft expenses. "
""
"That extra 15 minutes of browsing the airport shops could actually end up costing an airline thousands of dollars per flight! It’s a great reminder of how interconnected and finely tuned the global aviation system really is. "
""
"I want to create more posts that explore the hidden systems behind the travel industry. Which systems do you want me to share next?
posts.hook: Being 15 minutes late for a flight that costs you $70 could actually end up costing an airline upwards of $1,500… "

posts.full_text:
When we think about tourism spend, it’s easy to focus on arrivals, occupancy or visitor spend. But have you ever actually wondered what happens to a dollar once a tourist spends it? "
""
"A single dollar spent in the United States travels much further and faster than most people realise. "
""
"According to Trading Economics, $1 of travel spending generates roughly $1.73 in economic output. That’s the multiplier effect of tourism."
""
"Here’s how that dollar breaks down, based on national travel-spend data: "
""
"→ Transport (roughly 33-39%) "
"Transport is one of the biggest economic engines, with airlines, airports, logistics teams, mechanics and public transport systems all experiencing the impact of tourism almost instantly. When tourism rises, transport ecosystems scale with it, and when it slows down, these industries are often the first to feel the impact of it. "
""
"→ Food & Beverage Services (roughly 25%)"
"This is where tourism dollars have some of the biggest impacts locally, supporting chefs, servers, small vendors, suppliers and farmers. Food and beverage is one of the largest creators of entry-level jobs in the U.S., and tourism helps stabilise them. "
""
"→ Lodging (roughly 22%)"
"This area tends to be the most visible tourism category, but it receives a smaller share of the dollar than most people expect. But its economic reach is massive, supporting hotel workers, cleaning teams, tech vendors, maintenance crews and entire neighbourhood economies. "
""
"→ Entertainment & Shopping (roughly 17%)"
"This is where tourism connects with culture. This sector supports artists, performers, guides and retailers, and helps maintain the experiences that attract visitors in the first place. "
""
"→ Other (roughly 3%)"
"This often involves travel-related spending, like insurance, travel advisors and funding service ecosystems that help keep the industry moving in a safe way. These costs are what enable trips to happen in the first place. "
""
"This is why the travel industry is one of the greatest economic engines in the world, and I’m so excited and proud to be a part of it."
""
"For tourism boards and policymakers, this breakdown is essential when considering how to build better travel experiences. Because this not only increases demand but also amplifies the economic impact across an entire nation.

posts.full_text:
Business travel is about to be completely reshaped by AI. "
""
"We’re not just talking about AI booking a flight or a hotel, because that’s the simplest part of the transformation. The real shift is going to happen across everything else that surrounds the business travel journey, like the planning, preparation, on-trip decisions, performance and reporting. "
""
"Business travel is complex, expensive and highly regulated, and that’s exactly why I think AI will have its biggest impact here first. "
""
"Here’s where I think we’re going to see the biggest shifts:"
""
"→ AI will manage business travel before the trip begins:"
"Instead of spending hours searching and coordinating, business travellers will have AI agents that pre-emptively adjust itineraries based on schedules, align flights and hotels with global teams, pre-approve trips based on budget thresholds, flag policy exceptions automatically and secure approvals without the need for people to go back and forth. "
""
"Booking becomes the final step instead of the first one. "
""
"→ AI will optimise business travel around performance, not logistics:"
"For executives, founders and teams who move around a lot, AI will become the full performance coach - from personalised sleep, nutrition and recovery protocols to flight recommendations based on circadian rhythm and hotels ranked by productivity and noise levels."
""
"Business travel has always been built around logistics, but AI will rebuild it around human performance. "
""
"→ AI will become a full-service travel manager during the trip:"
"We’re heading towards AI agents that are capable of rebooking instantly during disruptions, filing expenses automatically in the background, tracking duty of care obligations like safety, risk and location, splitting costs for group travel and coordinating meetings, transport and hotel services without input. "
""
"This removes friction for business travellers and massively reduces operational overhead for employers. "
""
"→ AI will transform the on-ground business travel experience:"
"Once people arrive at their destinations, AI will build dynamic itineraries based on energy levels and meetings, anticipate needs, suggest ‘nearby recommendations’ for gaps in between meetings and connect travellers to local experiences that are aligned with business goals. "
""
"Business travel will become adaptive, personal and context-aware at every moment. "
""
"AI isn’t going to replace business travel entirely, but it will make it higher-value, lower-friction and significantly more productive. "
""
"If you’re a travel leader, I’d love to get your input on this. Which part of the AI shift do you think will have the biggest impact on business travel?
posts.hook: Business travel is about to be completely reshaped by AI. "

posts.full_text:
Tourism board marketing has looked the same for decades, but in the past couple of years, we’ve been witnessing a shift."
""
"It’s a shift that BD has been talking about for years, getting tourists to buy into a story through creators rather than investing in glossy TV ads that don’t resonate, as they once did."
""
"I’ve been sharing some of my favourite tourism board examples over the past couple of months, and today I wanted to spotlight three more:"
""
"1.⁠ ⁠Welcome to the Land of Chilled by MeetInNorway - Visit Norway"
"Norway has mastered the art of self-awareness in marketing. Instead of pretending to be something it’s not, Visit Norway leaned into what makes it unique - the cold, the calm, the quiet. "
""
"Most destinations try to compete on the same themes, but Norway differentiates by embracing its truth and turning it into a lifestyle people aspire to. Perfect example of a brand knowing its audience and building a story around real identity Anne-Signe Fagereng. "
""
"2.⁠ ⁠This Land is Calling by Saudi Tourism Authority | الهيئة السعودية للسياحة"
"With an ambitious goal of attracting 150 million tourists by 2030, Saudi Arabia released this campaign in 2024 to encourage visitors to explore the heart of Arabia. The clever part is how they balance global-scale storytelling with creator-driven content that feels personal, local and human. "
""
"A destination this big could easily default to glossy, cinematic advertising. But instead, they’re building emotional connections through real people and real narratives, which shows how creator storytelling can shift perception and accelerate a country’s position as one of the fastest-growing tourism destinations in the world. "
""
"3.⁠ ⁠“Portugal, an unwritten recipe” by Visit Portugal"
"Visit Portugal released this campaign as part of a broader plan to internationalise Portuguese gastronomy as a distinctive way to promote the destination. Food is a huge driver of travel intent, and Portugal has used this to turn it into an open invitation for travellers to participate and shape the experience themselves. "
""
"By using food as an open door to the country’s creativity, heritage and community, Visit Portugal is building emotional connections through a universal language that can scale globally. "
""
"Each of these examples demonstrates how tourism has evolved from promotion to participation, something I predict we’ll see more of in the coming years."
""
"Do you remember any of these great campaigns? What’s your best example of a tourism board differentiating itself?
posts.hook: Tourism board marketing has looked the same for decades, but in the past couple of years, we’ve been witnessing a shift."

Jet2’s ‘Nothing Beats a Jet2 Holiday’ soundtrack might have become its most profitable asset this year…"

"This summer, Jet2.com and Jet2holidays’ infamous Jess Glynne soundtrack became a viral meme, exploding all over TikTok and generating 80 billion views across user-generated videos."
""
"When a brand asset is being used in unexpected or even undesirable ways, like the soundtrack to fights or arrests, you’d think the immediate reaction would be to step in and shut it down to ‘protect the brand’."
""
"But Jet2 let it play out."
""
"And, according to Marketing Week, these were the results:"
""
"→ 750,000 additional passengers in just six months"
"→ Group revenue up 5% to £5.34 billion"
"→ myJet2 loyalty membership up by 62% to 8.4 million subscribers"
"→ Operating profit up by 2% to £715.2 million"
""
"All from a completely unplanned trend that amplified a brand asset in ways paid media could never have done."
""
"It didn’t come without risk, as consumer perception data shows Jet2’s quality score dropped from +17.7% in January to +7.2% by October, its lowest point in the year."
""
"But, in the middle of all the chaos, Jet2 did something that lots of brands try and resist: you can’t control social media culture, the best you can do is collaborate with it, because when you do, the commercial impact is far greater than anything you can buy."
""
"In this case, a meme widened their funnel, boosted loyalty and drove real passengers, revenue and shareholder value."
""
"I’d love to hear your thoughts. Do you think it was the right call to let the internet do what it does best? 🙏

posts.full_text:
When we started BD, New York traditional media still dominated the global stage. Hearst & Condé Nast had their huge, imposing office buildings, their executives were driven around the city in luxury limousines, and their reputation for being the most influential players in the city was fearsome."
""
"Social media did not have a seat at the table, as back then, print/website still defined influence. Media Executives controlled distribution and decided which stories the world saw. They were the guys and girls everybody wanted to impress, controlling culture and advertising dollars."
""
"Being politely persistent, I managed to meet with all of them. And all of them thought I was a waste of time and told me to my face."
""
"That all changed one day when I met an amazing British executive called Kevin Heery. He was SVP of Digital at Time Inc., overseeing growth for Travel & Leisure and many others. He got it straight away and gave me a shot when every single other media brand said no. He gave me a budget and said, 'Have a go at growing our Instagram account and helping us create a media product'."
""
"I didn’t tell him at the time, but certain team members in that organisation gave me so much hassle and tried to make me fail at every turn, but we persevered and smashed it for them, growing the accounts to hundreds of thousands of followers and building high-quality travel content which they sold in their media packages."
""
"It’s funny how only one person believing in you can change the course of your life, and as I’ve said over and over again, it’s often your early clients that play as important a role as your early employees."
""
"All these years later, the power dynamic between traditional media and social media has completely reversed. Back then, print was the gatekeeper and social was the experiment. Today, social IS the media, and the best marketers in the new world are generally individuals who know their audiences and the platforms, not the institutions."
""
"Kevin has been the Chief Product Officer at Priceline now for almost a decade, so it looks like the gamble he took has paid off for both of us :)"
""
"📸 Mandarin Oriental, in New York

It's the time of year when travel brands start sharing the data which tells us where travel is going next year."
""
"For all of us in travel marketing, it’s a chance to learn and create the strategies we think will perform."
""
"I've been reviewing all the reports I can get my hands on, and Skyscanner’s new 2026 Trends Report gives us a good early look at how we’re evolving. Great work Bryan Batista and the Skyscanner team! "
""
"1.⁠ ⁠People are ready to spend more."
"Probably not a surprise to those in the industry, despite the economic headwinds we’re reading about in the news. 37% of travellers plan to increase their flight budgets next year, and 31% will spend more on accommodation. Typically, we are seeing fewer trips, but deeper, more meaningful ones, with multiple destinations covered and a slightly longer duration."
""
"2.⁠ ⁠Experiences and comfort are taking priority."
"45% of travellers plan to book tours and activities, and a third are choosing multi-city trips. Many are creating their own itineraries, completely personalised to their needs. We've been seeing exciting growth in the search queries within the Layla AI Trip Planner for hyper-personalised itineraries, which are only getting better as our technology improves."
""
"3.⁠ ⁠AI is impacting decision-making."
"Obvious? Perhaps not in the way you'd think. Skyscanner's research found 49% of travellers worry about the accuracy of AI travel tools, while 24% feel overwhelmed by too many choices. Yes, they are saving time, but is it time well spent if we don’t trust the results?"
""
"The AI discussion dominates travel trend reporting, with both positive and negative sentiment relatively equal. I for one have found AI tools to be a huge benefit in my travel planning (and all other areas of my life) and whilst they aren’t yet perfect, they’re getting better faster than I could have imagined.
posts.hook: It's the time of year when travel brands start sharing the data which tells us where travel is going next year."
